articles.title: Amazon reportedly pays $120 million to stream the Emmys for free
articles.summary: Amazon has paid a reported $120 million for the rights to stream the Emmys on Prime Video starting in 2027.
articles.body: The Emmys have a new home — and it looks like Amazon paid plenty for the rights. The awards show and Amazon announced a six-year deal that will move the Emmys from its traditional broadcast television home to Prime Video. The shift begins with the 2027 ceremony, which will air next September, though you won’t actually have to sign up for Prime Video to watch it. The announcement instead says that the stream “will be free to view for audiences worldwide.” According to Deadline, Amazon paid around $20-25 million per year for the rights, making the deal worth upwards of $120 million. “Our broadcast partners have been tremendous stewards of the Emmys for many years, helping to build them into the cultural institution they are today,” Cris Abrego, chair of the Television Academy, said in a statement. “Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year.” The news comes as streaming services are looking for tentpole live events to add to their offerings, and awards shows have become a particularly popular choice. Netflix snapped up the rights to the SAG awards, while the Oscars will be moving to YouTube in 2029. Meanwhile, streaming services have also come to dominate the Emmys. At this year’s awards, Apple TV had the most wins of any network, led by Widow’s Bay, which won a total of 14 awards.

articles.title: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery complete $110 billion media megamerger
articles.summary: Paramount has closed its $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, putting major film studios, networks, and streaming services under one roof.
articles.body: Paramount has completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, forming a combined company known as Skydance. The merger officially puts Paramount and WBD’s film studios, along with major networks and brands like HBO, CBS News, and CNN, under one roof. The road to the media megamerger has been a rocky one for Paramount, which secured an agreement in February after waging a months-long battle against Netflix for WBD. Since then, it has faced criticism from both lawmakers and Hollywood talent about the negative impact of media consolidation. Paramount cleared its last major hurdle last month, as it settled with 12 states that sued to block the deal over antitrust concerns. Under the settlement, Skydance must release a minimum number of theatrical films over the next five years, starting with 30 in years one and two. It must also spend at least $300 million more on production in the US compared to what the companies spent last year combined. David Ellison will lead Skydance alongside Ynon Kreiz, the former chairman and CEO of Mattel. “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in the announcement. “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality.”

articles.title: Emmy Awards exit broadcast television for Amazon’s Prime Video
articles.summary: The television industry’s marquee awards show is heading to streaming starting next year.
articles.body: The television industry’s marquee awards show is heading to streaming starting next year. Amazon’s Prime Video platform will be the “exclusive global home” of the Emmy Awards for a six-year period starting in 2027, the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences announced Tuesday morning. “Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share,” said Cris Abrego, the chair of the Television Academy. “Now Prime Video audiences in more than 200 countries will be able to experience the Emmys live with no subscription required.” The terms of the deal were not disclosed. The Emmys has been a mainstay of broadcast television for decades, with academy heads following a “Wheel Deal” system that rotated telecast distribution rights among ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. The move comes nearly a year after the organization behind the Oscars said Hollywood’s top awards show would move to YouTube starting in 2029, after the film academy’s deal with ABC concludes. ABC has aired the Academy Awards since the 1970s. Netflix helped inaugurate the trend, scooping up rights to SAG-AFTRA’s Actor Awards in 2024. The deals illustrate streaming’s growing dominance in the television and video ecosystem. In July, 49% of all U.S. television viewing was on a streaming platform, according to statistics published by Nielsen, compared to 19.5% on broadcast networks. The most recent Emmys telecast drew 6.8 million total viewers across NBC, Peacock and other digital platforms on Sept. 14 — a roughly 10% decline from the 7.59 million viewers who tuned in for the 2025 ceremony on CBS. In a news release, Amazon and the Television Academy said the new distribution pact would turn the Emmys into “a year-round cultural celebration,” with Prime Video “delivering new experiences and entry points” for TV fans. “Amazon shares our deep respect for the history of the Emmys and brings the investment, innovation and scale to help us shape their next chapter,” Abrego said.

articles.title: Richard Gere confronts Hollywood fame, ego and greed as 'dark clouds' that threaten inner peace
articles.summary: Richard Gere reveals how more than 40 years of practicing Buddhism helps him battle ego, greed and jealousy in his decades-long Hollywood career.
articles.body: Richard Gere has spent decades in Hollywood, but he hasn’t let fame go to his head — at least not without a fight. The actor serves as an executive producer of the documentary "Wisdom of Happiness," which explores the Dalai Lama’s teachings and the pursuit of lasting joy. Gere has practiced Buddhism for more than 40 years. Asked how he keeps fame and ego in check after decades in Hollywood, Gere admitted he isn’t immune. TIM ROBBINS TURNS TO AYAHUASCA AFTER FEELING 'CONSUMED BY ANGER' OVER CANCEL CULTURE "Everyone goes through that," the 77-year-old told Fox News Digital. "Everyone has the forces of greed, anger, self-cherishing, impatience, jealousy, the whole gamut. Everyone has that. So I think from Buddhist training and looking at these afflictive emotions and seeing where they’re coming from, they’re not innate in me. They’re kind of add-ons to basic clarity of the mind." "It’s said that the mind is clear and knowing, so clear, vast, no limits," he said. "It has a sense of knowing, wisdom. The other stuff is just kind of add-ons, like dark clouds coming through. They come, and they go." Gere also isn’t looking to Hollywood for happiness. The longtime leading man has learned that the perks only go so far. WATCH: RICHARD GERE SHARES THE LIFE LESSON THAT BRINGS HIM HAPPINESS "Well, clearly, happiness and peace [don’t] come from the outside," he explained. "It comes from inside all of us, and it’s there. You don’t have to create that. But I think it’s removing the bad habits, removing the causes that make us feel bad ultimately. But we’re in control of our experience for sure. We’re responsible for it. If you don’t like the way things are, you change it. And all things are changeable. They’re changing all the time anyhow. Probably when we fight the change is when we feel the worst." For Gere, that also means questioning how much material success really matters. "Well, what’s really important? Is it what I own or what I am?" Gere said. "I’m not going to get anything from the outside that is permanently going to make me happy." "Momentarily, yes, like a piece of chocolate, but that’s not permanent, is it?" he joked. Gere has also found happiness far from the spotlight. These days, the star splits his time between Spain and upstate New York. "Well, Spain is my wife’s country, so she gets super happy there," he said with a smile. "And I’ll tell you when my wife’s super happy, I’m super happy. And I grew up in the Northeast. I feel very close to that. And my early family memories, and my grandfather’s farm in Pennsylvania, I think, had a huge impact. It still does." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Gere and his wife, Spanish publicist Alejandra Silva, have two sons together. Silva also has a son from a previous relationship, while Gere shares his eldest son, Homer, with ex-wife Carey Lowell. "My first son is 26 now," Gere said. "And I talked to him about what he’s going through right now. And I remember myself as a 25-year-old, 26-year-old person. Of course, my concerns were different. I certainly was more susceptible to what people said and thought about me and about anything else. And frankly, I don’t care that much about it right now, what anyone thinks or says." Looking back, Gere recalled growing up in "an extraordinary Christian family" with roots in a small town in Pennsylvania. His father, Homer Gere, spent his childhood milking cows, and both his parents instilled in him the importance of helping others — values he carried with him when he discovered Buddhism in his 20s. "I grew up with that imprint, I think, from my dad and my mom, but there was something about Buddhism that kind of went beyond that and was willing to explore the larger questions," Gere said. "What is reality? What am I? What is a human being?" "Am I capable of much greater things than just worrying about myself?" he continued. "And certainly, Buddhism wanted to engage those things [for me]." But the lessons Gere learned from farmers have never left him. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "I think that farmers have a balanced sense of the universe," he said. "When the rain doesn’t come, who are you going to complain to? It’s about acceptance of things. It doesn’t make you happy when the rain doesn’t come, or it comes too much, but the forces of the universe are just the way they are. And along with it, hard work." "Farmers work really hard," Gere said. "I still have the kerosene lantern that my grandfather used. He would get up at four o’clock in the morning and go do the first milking of the cows." Gere said he sees that same work ethic in the Dalai Lama. "He still gets up at 3:30 in the morning, does his practice, works on his mind, works on his heart, works on his motivation, purifies himself every day," Gere said. "He’s a human being, and he continues, as I said, to work on himself," he continued. "If we want to achieve what he’s achieved, to become really such an extraordinary, genuine person, we’ve got to do the work." Gere said his connection to "Wisdom of Happiness" became deeply personal after he and Silva first watched the film together in New York. "And I thought for his 90th birthday, this would be a great summation of an extraordinary life, well-lived, a meaningful life dedicated to others." But as the film came together, Gere said its message began to feel increasingly urgent. "In the time it took to finish the editing and finish the film, I think the world continued to fall apart in a very challenging, dark way," he said. Gere said he hopes the documentary reminds people they have the capacity for compassion. "The beginning point, and maybe the end point, is basic kindness, a warm heart and generosity of spirit," he said. articles.title: Qué va a pasar ahora con HBO Max tras la compra de Warner Bros.: una decisión que afecta a millones de usuarios
articles.standfirst: Se desconoce si desaparecerá o se acabará fusionando con Paramount+
articles.summary: Se desconoce si desaparecerá o se acabará fusionando con Paramount+
articles.body: Este martes, 6 de octubre, Paramount Skydance completó la adquisición de Warner Bros. Discovery por 110.000 millones de dólares. Se ha completado así una operación que se anunció en febrero de este mismo año y estaba pendiente de completar los diversos procesos antes de hacerse efectiva en una fecha que se anunció a finales de septiembre y que finalmente se ha cumplido. El nuevo grupo reúne a Warner Bros., Paramount Pictures, CNN, DC, HBO, CBS o HBO. Sin embargo, una de las principales incógnitas que deja esta transacción es saber qué acabará pasando con los millones de usuarios de HBO Max, algo de lo que no hay novedades, al menos, hasta ahora. Los usuarios se preguntan si HBO Max podría desaparecer o si se fusionará con Paramount+. Sin embargo, desde la propia plataforma de streaming confirmaron que, por ahora, no habrá cambios inmediatos en su aplicación, sus contenidos, sus suscripciones ni sus precios, por lo que los usuarios podrán usar el servicio con normalidad. Asimismo, tampoco ha salido una nueva plataforma que mezcle a HBO Max y a Paramount+. Eso sí, la compañía sí que podría contemplar la posibilidad de ofrecer opciones conjuntas en el futuro, pero no hay una fecha ni un modelo concretado. Esto es algo que también se puede aplicar con el catálogo: los contenidos de Paramount+ no pasarán automáticamente a HBO Max tras la operación. De esta manera, este nuevo conglomerado tendrá así dos servicios de streaming de grandes magnitudes bajo su control. Por ello, aún la estrategia aún está por definir, lo que se sabe es que los suscriptores de HBO Max no tienen que hacer nada por ahora. La plataforma seguirá funcionando igual y si hubiera cualquier cambio se le comunicará de manera previa a todos los usuarios.

articles.title: White executive fired after wearing cornrows, triggering legal fight over Maryland's CROWN Act
articles.summary: Attorney Jeremy Eldridge said Maryland's CROWN Act could apply after the Baltimore Rock Opera Society fired a White executive over wearing cornrows.
articles.body: A White Baltimore arts executive was fired in September from the Baltimore Rock Opera Society after backlash over her decision to wear cornrows following a trip to Burning Man. Attorney Jeremy Eldridge said the circumstances of the firing of Kelly Carnes could raise discrimination questions under Maryland's CROWN Act. Eldridge said the organization’s public statements about Carnes' hairstyle could become relevant evidence if she challenges her dismissal. "Had the Baltimore Rock Opera simply separated from this individual without providing a discriminatory reason; the timeline would be all of the evidence that the fired employee would have," he told WBFF Fox45 Baltimore. "But here, when you're making comments publicly that lean into the discriminatory allegation made by the fired employees, that itself could be evidence of the fact that you were terminated wrongfully, meaning that it's discrimination under the crown." WHITE DEVELOPER SUES BALTIMORE MAYOR, CITY COUNCIL CLAIMING HE WAS FIRED BECAUSE OF HIS RACE Carnes directed Fox News Digital to WBFF's reporting when contacted about the controversy. She began serving as executive director of the Baltimore Rock Opera Society, known as BROS, on Sept. 8. The organization formally announced her appointment less than a week later, touting her more than 21 years of experience in arts leadership, nonprofit strategy, communications, fundraising and operations. Carnes said she had her hair put into cornrows as a protective hairstyle while attending Burning Man in Nevada’s desert. After she returned, a video showing her with the hairstyle at a BROS event prompted complaints that a White woman wearing cornrows constituted cultural appropriation. BROS publicly acknowledged the backlash after removing the video, saying it had received concerns from members of its community and was taking the matter seriously. The organization also said it regretted removing the video without an explanation. "We have received many heartfelt and concerned messages from members of our community regarding a video circulated on social media showing our new Executive Director, who is White, wearing cornrows at a recent BROS public event," the organization said, according to WBAL. "We share the weight of these concerns and take this matter seriously." WASHINGTON POST ORDERED TO REINSTATE COLUMNIST KAREN ATTIAH AFTER BEING TERMINATED OVER CHARLIE KIRK POSTS The organization said it would revise its anti-discrimination policy to address cultural representation and dress, require anti-racism leadership training and create a working group focused on racial equity and inclusion, according to The Baltimore Banner. Carnes said that the board advised her not to attend a town hall convened to discuss the controversy. She said she was dismissed days later and was told only that she was "not a good fit." Eldridge said determining whether the firing violated Maryland law would require establishing what actually motivated the organization’s decision. "In evaluating whether the CROWN Act applies, meaning whether there was discrimination and whether this individual was terminated as for a discriminatory reason because of a hairstyle, we still have to deal with there are two competing narratives," Eldridge said. NEW YORK TIMES SUED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER ALLEGED 'DEI-RELATED' EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION Maryland enacted its CROWN Act in 2020. State law now defines race for purposes of anti-discrimination protections to include "traits associated with race," including hair texture, Afro hairstyles and protective hairstyles. "Protective hairstyles" under the statute include braids, twists and locks. The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights says the law applies to employment practices including hiring, workplace conditions, discipline and termination. Fox News Digital reached out to the commission for comment, but did not immediately receive a response. The statute does not itself resolve whether Carnes' firing was unlawful, leaving the circumstances and motivation behind the termination central to any potential discrimination claim. The turmoil has extended beyond Carnes' departure. Four of BROS’ six board members, including its chair, are expected to leave the organization at the end of the year, according to an email obtained by The Baltimore Banner. articles.title: Emmys will move from broadcast TV to Prime Video in 2027
articles.summary: Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will be able to watch the awards show on the platform.
articles.body:
Amazon announced on Tuesday that Prime Video will be the new home for the Emmy Awards, marking another major Hollywood awards show’s move from broadcast television to streaming. This will also be the first time that the ceremony has had a dedicated home, as the show rotated across broadcasters like ABC, CBS, Fox, and NBC over the past seven decades.

Prime Video will stream the awards show worldwide for six years for free, starting in 2027, where it will go live in over 240 countries and territories. Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will also be able to watch the awards show on the Prime Video platform.

The terms of the deal were not disclosed.

The move comes as the Emmys face potential viewership declines, as more of its audience moves to streaming services. This year’s ratings for the 78th primetime Emmy Awards on NBC were down nearly 10% from the year prior, after a couple of years of growth, the AP reported . However, the telecast’s 6.87 million viewers this year were higher than its all-time low of 4.3 million in January 2024.

The Emmys aren’t the only major awards show making the shift to streaming. Last year, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal giving YouTube the rights to stream the Oscars beginning in 2029, while Netflix has streamed the Screen Actors Guild Awards since 2024.

articles.title: Oscar De La Hoya reveals why he didn’t attend Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn fight: ‘I was going to be set up’
articles.summary: Oscar De La Hoya explains his absence from Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn
articles.body:
Oscar De La Hoya has no regrets about not attending Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn.

Last month, Garcia knocked out Benn in arguably the biggest fight of his career. The bout was a co-promotion between De La Hoya's Golden Boy Promotions and Zuffa Boxing, but the Golden Boy CEO was noticeably absent from most of the promotion of the event. That extended to the actual fight night, and afterward, Garcia admitted to being disappointed that De La Hoya didn't show up to support him . But the boxing Hall of Famer had his reasons.

"I wasn't going to show up to be embarrassed," De La Hoya told Fight Hub TV. "It was a Zuffa f*cking event. A 'Zuffa event,' a 'Turki event' [doing quotation marks with his hands]. I was not going to show up and be embarrassed, because that's exactly what they were going to do to me. I was not going to do that. So I made the wise decision to not go."

De La Hoya has a long history of bad blood with Zuffa Boxing CEO Dana White, which has only grown since White moved into boxing. And per reports on the Garcia-Benn event, De La Hoya was denied his appropriate ringside credential for the event as co-promoter of the fight, meaning he would be seated in the crowd. White denied these claims, but De La Hoya certainly feels that had he attended, it would not have been as part of the promotion.

"Oh yeah, so much shit happened in those dealings, in those contracts, but let's just say I'm glad I didn't go because I was going to be set up," De La Hoya said. "You saw Teofimo [Lopez], how they didn't allow him in the ring to have a faceoff with Ryan, and embarrassed him not going up there. It's like, I'm not going to be embarrassed going to an event where my fighter is participating in. I just wasn't going to do it.

"It would have been embarrassing. It would have created distractions. It would have been a mess."

De La Hoya says that embarrassment wasn't just aimed at him either, but at his fighters, too. While Garcia was the event headliner — with rumors abounding that the longtime Golden Boy product might make the move to Zuffa at the conclusion of his current deal — De La Hoya says that his other fighters were given short shrift, not to mention his staff that worked the event.

"Nothing is finished until you finish it. And I'm not done yet. I haven't even started, let's put it that way," De La Hoya said. "But yeah, my personnel were complaining about how they were being treated wrongly and how the event was just not professional. It was bad.

"How can you put Alexis Rocha with [Jose] Ramirez on the second fight of the night? They fought at what, 2 p.m.? What an embarrassment for the fighters, and how damaging that can be to the fighter's reputation. Putting two world-class fighters in the start of the evening is not professional. …

"Most likely [they did this on purpose]. Absolutely, I believe so. 'Oh, those are Oscar's fighters, and they're Golden Boy? Let's put them first so nobody will see them.' Absolutely. I'm not born yesterday. I know how this works."
